tiles.title: Distribution Shape, Outliers, and Frequency Distributions
tiles.summary: Learn to read a distribution's shape as right-skewed, left-skewed, or symmetric; reason about outliers; and translate a frequency table into statements about where delivery times cluster and where rare values sit.

steps.title: Which way does the tail point?
steps.lede: Most delivery times cluster in a narrow band — but a few orders take much longer. The direction that long stretch points is what analysts call the shape of a distribution.

blocks.text: Consider nine QuickShip delivery times: 18, 20, 22, 22, 26, 28, 34, 41, 52 minutes. Most orders finish between 18 and 28 minutes, but the remaining values climb gradually toward 52. That overall pattern — where the bulk of the values sit and which direction the data trails off toward — is what analysts call the shape of a distribution.

A distribution is right-skewed when it has a longer tail trailing off to the right, and left-skewed when it has a longer tail trailing off to the left. This delivery-time batch is right-skewed: the bulk of the values sit between 18 and 28 minutes, and 34, 41, and 52 form a gradually lengthening tail trailing off to the right.

blocks.title: Right-skewed distribution: QuickShip delivery times
blocks.alt_text: A bar chart showing the QuickShip delivery-time sample with bars tallest at 18–28 min and a long tail trailing right toward 52 min — labelled Right-skewed. An arrow marks the long tail.

steps.title: Symmetric distributions and what skew does to the mean
steps.lede: When a distribution has no long tail, the mean and median sit close together. A skewed tail pulls the mean away from the median.

blocks.text: A distribution is symmetric when it trails off by roughly equal amounts in both directions. If the delivery-time batch had values spread evenly above and below its centre — some orders a bit faster and some a bit slower than 24 minutes, with no single value trailing far off in either direction — that would be a symmetric distribution.

The mean is more affected by extreme observations — such as those in the long tail of a skewed distribution — than the median, which is more robust to them. In the right-skewed delivery-time batch, the mean (about 29.2 minutes) sits above the median (26 minutes), pulled upward by the gradual right-hand tail.

steps.title: Symmetric, left-skewed and right-skewed distributions
steps.lede: Watch how the direction the long tail points — not where the tall bars sit — names the skew.

blocks.group_title: Telling symmetric, left-skewed and right-skewed apart

segments.label: Symmetric, left-skewed and right-skewed distributions told apart by which way the tail trails
segments.summary: Shows three of six example charts and names each shape. Housefly lengths form a symmetric distribution: a line down the middle gives two mirror-image halves, and real data is usually only roughly symmetric. Dates on pennies have a long tail to the left with the high points on the right, so the distribution is left-skewed. Representatives per state have most values low and a tail stretching right, so it is right-skewed. The narrator reads the bars out loud, so no earlier chart-reading is needed. The clip stops before any link between shape and the mean or median.

bridge.before: Watch how the side the long tail points to, not where the tall bars sit, names the skew. The clip's examples are bar charts of counts; Devspace's text works from lists of values instead.
bridge.after: The clip never links shape to the mean and median. The text fills that gap: a long tail pulls the mean toward it, away from the median.

steps.title: Skew and the mean vs. median
steps.lede: A delivery-time dataset has a long tail trailing to the right. How does that affect the mean compared with the median?

steps.title: Classify the shape of a delivery-time distribution
steps.lede: Look at the QuickShip delivery-time sample. Decide whether the distribution is right-skewed, left-skewed, or symmetric, and say whether the mean should sit above or below the median.

steps.title: Spotting an outlier and deciding what to do with it
steps.lede: One delivery in the batch took 80 minutes — far beyond the rest. Spotting it is only the first step; reasoning about why it's there is what matters.

blocks.text: In a seven-order delivery batch — 18, 20, 22, 22, 26, 28, 80 minutes — that 80-minute order stands out from the rest. An outlier is an observation that appears extreme relative to the rest of the data, and that single delivery clearly qualifies.

Examining a dataset for outliers can help identify strong skew in the distribution, spot possible data collection or data entry errors, and reveal interesting properties of the data. For that 80-minute order, this could mean noticing the skew it creates, checking whether someone mistyped "8.0" as "80," or discovering something genuinely unusual — like the delivery being stuck behind a road closure.

Examine an outlier to judge whether it is a possible data collection or data entry error or a genuine observation; a genuine outlier should not be removed without a very good reason. That means checking the order record itself — was 80 actually logged, or should it have been 8.0? — before deciding what to do about it.

An outlier is not automatically a data error: it may instead be a genuine, correct observation. If the driver really did take 80 minutes because of a road closure, that is real information about that specific delivery — not something to delete just because the value looks unusual next to the rest of the batch.

blocks.caption: Seven QuickShip delivery records. The 80-minute order (ORD-009) is highlighted — it stands out from the 18–28 minute cluster and warrants investigation before any decision.

steps.title: What should you do with an outlier?
steps.lede: A delivery record shows 80 minutes — far beyond the rest of the batch. What is the right first action?

steps.title: Find and reason about the outlier in the delivery dataset
steps.lede: Scan the QuickShip delivery records. Mark the extreme value, then choose whether to keep, investigate, or exclude it — and explain why.

steps.title: From a list of times to a histogram and frequency table
steps.lede: Instead of listing every delivery time one by one, group them into ranges and count how many orders fall into each range.

blocks.text: Instead of listing every delivery time one by one, imagine grouping a full day's 21 QuickShip deliveries into 10-minute ranges and counting how many orders fall into each range. That grouping turns a long list into a compact summary.

A histogram groups numerical values into bins and represents the count of observations in each bin as a bar; taller bars show where the data values are relatively more common. For the day's 21 deliveries, the tallest bar sits over the 20–30 minute bin, and a much shorter bar sits far out over the 80–90 minute bin.

The table of counts of observations in each bin, which a histogram displays as bars, is called a frequency table. For that same day: 10–20 min, 4 orders; 20–30 min, 9 orders; 30–40 min, 5 orders; 40–50 min, 2 orders; 50–80 min, 0 orders; 80–90 min, 1 order.

blocks.title: Frequency table and histogram of 21 QuickShip delivery times
blocks.alt_text: A bar chart with delivery-time bins on the horizontal axis (10–20 min, 20–30 min, 30–40 min, 40–50 min, 50–80 min, 80–90 min) and order count on the vertical axis. The tallest bar is 20–30 min with 9 orders, marked as the peak. The 80–90 min bar is very short (1 order), showing the far-out delivery.

steps.title: From stacked measurements to a frequency table and histogram
steps.lede: Watch how measurements are grouped into bins and stacked into bars, then turned into a histogram from a frequency table.

blocks.group_title: From stacked measurements to a frequency table and histogram

segments.label: How a histogram is built: measurements grouped into bins and stacked into bars
segments.summary: An animated explanation of why histograms exist. Measurements of height pile up as dots until they overlap and hide each other. Stacking only identical values doesn't help much, so the range of values is divided into bins and the measurements in each bin are stacked. The result is a histogram, where a taller stack means more measurements fell into that bin.

segments.label: From a frequency table to a histogram: drawing the bars and reading the mode
segments.summary: Starts from a finished frequency table of test scores grouped into ranges and turns it into a histogram on a whiteboard: score ranges go along the bottom, counts go up the side, and the bars touch with no gaps. Bar heights follow the table, from 1 in the lowest range up to 5 in the 80s. The presenter then reads the shape, a long tail on the left, so skewed left, and says the mode is the range with the highest frequency, here 80 to 89. A mix-up over which axis holds what is corrected on the spot.

bridge.before: Clip 1 shows bins and stacking; clip 2 turns a frequency table into bars and reads the peak. Clip 2 calls the table a 'frequency distribution table' and says 'negative skew' for left-skewed.
bridge.after: Clip 1 covers only bins and bars; clip 2 adds the frequency table and the mode as the highest-count range. Devspace's text also allows a peak that spans several neighbouring bins.

steps.title: Reading the modal bin
steps.lede: The tallest bar in a histogram marks the range where observations are most concentrated.

blocks.text: A mode appears in a histogram as a prominent peak: a bin, or region of neighbouring bins, where observations are noticeably more concentrated than elsewhere. In the 21-order frequency table, the 20–30 minute bin — with 9 of 21 orders — is that peak.

steps.title: Reading a frequency table
steps.lede: A frequency table shows: 10–20 min: 4 orders; 20–30 min: 9 orders; 30–40 min: 5 orders; 40–50 min: 2 orders; 50–80 min: 0 orders; 80–90 min: 1 order. Which bin has the most orders?

steps.title: Read the delivery-time frequency table
steps.lede: Use the QuickShip frequency table to name the modal bin, describe the spread, and say whether the shape is skewed.

steps.title: What you've learned
steps.lede: Three ideas that let you describe any batch of numbers at a glance.

blocks.text: A distribution's shape — right-skewed, left-skewed, or symmetric — describes which direction the data trails off. A long tail pulls the mean toward it, away from the median. An outlier is an extreme observation: investigate it before acting, because it may be a genuine event rather than an error. A frequency table or histogram translates raw counts into a picture of where deliveries cluster and where rare values sit.

blocks.title: Up next: Correlation and Its Limits
blocks.text: In the next tile you'll ask whether two numeric columns — like distance and delivery time — tend to move together, and learn how to measure the strength and direction of that relationship.

remediation_steps.title: Skew direction: a clear contrast
remediation_steps.lede: Compare two delivery batches — one with a tail trailing right, one with a tail trailing left.

blocks.text: Batch A: 18, 20, 22, 22, 26, 28, 34, 41, 52 minutes. Most values sit at the low end; the tail trails right — right-skewed. Batch B: 30, 38, 44, 48, 50, 52, 52, 54, 56 minutes. Most values sit at the high end; the tail trails left — left-skewed. The tail direction, not where the tall bars sit, names the skew.

remediation_steps.title: Error vs. genuine event: a clear contrast
remediation_steps.lede: Two 80-minute deliveries — same number, different explanations.

blocks.text: Case 1: The driver's app logged "80" but the actual time was 8 minutes — a data-entry error. Removing it is justified once confirmed. Case 2: The driver really did take 80 minutes because of a road closure — a genuine event. Removing it would hide real information. The same extreme value can be either; checking the record decides which.

remediation_steps.title: Reading a frequency table: bar height = count
remediation_steps.lede: Each row in the frequency table is one bar in the histogram.

blocks.text: Frequency table: 10–20 min → 4 orders; 20–30 min → 9 orders; 30–40 min → 5 orders. In the histogram, the 20–30 min bar is the tallest (9 orders), the 10–20 min bar is shorter (4 orders), and the 30–40 min bar sits in between (5 orders). Bar height equals the count in that bin — nothing more.

tiles.title: Correlation Between Two Variables
tiles.summary: Read a correlation coefficient's sign and magnitude to describe the direction and strength of a linear relationship, rank pairwise correlations by magnitude, and restate correlational findings as associations rather than causal claims.

steps.title: Does Distance Predict Delivery Time?
steps.lede: When two numeric columns move together, correlation gives you a single number that captures how strongly — and in which direction — they're linked.

blocks.text: QuickShip records two numbers for every delivery: distance in kilometres and delivery time in minutes. Do farther orders tend to take longer? Correlation answers that question with a single value that always sits between −1 and +1.

blocks.title: Distance vs. Delivery Time: Positive Correlation
blocks.alt_text: Scatter plot showing delivery orders. Points trend upward from left to right, indicating that as distance increases, delivery time also tends to increase — a positive correlation.

blocks.text: Correlation, which always takes values between −1 and +1, describes the strength of the linear relationship between two numeric variables. In a positive association, higher values of one variable tend to go with higher values of the other. In a negative association, higher values of one variable tend to go with lower values of the other.

steps.title: Scatter Patterns and the Correlation Coefficient
steps.lede: See how the shape of a scatter plot maps to values between −1 and +1.

steps.title: Reading Strength — and One Important Limit
steps.lede: Knowing how close a value sits to −1, 0, or +1 tells you the strength. But correlation only measures straight-line relationships.

blocks.text: A correlation near +1 indicates a strong positive linear relationship; near −1, a strong negative one; near 0, little or no linear relationship. In the QuickShip data, distance and delivery time come out to 0.82 — close to +1, so farther deliveries tend to take longer.

Correlation quantifies the strength of a linear relationship only. A nonlinear relationship can be strong even when its correlation value looks weak — so a value near 0 doesn't automatically mean the two variables are unrelated; it may mean their relationship isn't a straight-line one.

steps.title: Positive or Negative?
steps.lede: Test your reading of correlation direction.

steps.title: What Correlation Can't Tell You
steps.lede: Confirm you know the linear-only limit of correlation.

steps.title: Read Correlation Values in the QuickShip Data
steps.lede: Given correlation values for QuickShip delivery pairs, state the direction and strength of each relationship.

steps.title: Ranking Relationships by Magnitude
steps.lede: When you have several correlation values, magnitude — not sign — decides which relationship is strongest.

blocks.text: QuickShip records distance, package weight, and delivery time for every order. Their pairwise correlations are: distance and delivery time, 0.82; weight and delivery time, −0.41; distance and weight, −0.38.

blocks.caption: Pairwise Pearson correlations for QuickShip delivery variables. Compare magnitudes to rank relationship strength.

blocks.text: The strength of a correlation is judged by its magnitude — the absolute value. Comparing the three pairs: |0.82| is the strongest, |−0.41| is next, and |−0.38| is the weakest. Even though −0.41 is the lowest number, its magnitude makes it slightly stronger than −0.38.

steps.title: A Strong Correlation Doesn't Rule Out a Third Variable
steps.lede: A variable correlated with both sides of a pair can produce an association that isn't a direct link.

blocks.text: A confounding variable is correlated with both of two other variables being studied, so it can produce an association between them that is not a direct link. Distance is correlated with both weight and delivery time — so the −0.41 between weight and delivery time doesn't by itself mean weight directly drives delivery time; distance could be behind both.

steps.title: Could a Third Variable Explain This?
steps.lede: Test your understanding of confounding variables.

steps.title: Rank the QuickShip Correlations by Strength
steps.lede: Use the correlation matrix to rank the three variable pairs from strongest to weakest relationship.

steps.title: Moving Together Is Not the Same as Causing
steps.lede: A correlation tells you two things move together — it never tells you that one makes the other happen.

blocks.text: Suppose an analysis finds that orders with the delivery app's priority toggle switched on correlate with faster delivery times. That's an interesting pattern — but does flipping the toggle actually speed things up?

Association does not imply causation: a correlation between two variables does not by itself establish that one causes the other. Finding that priority orders and fast deliveries move together in the data doesn't prove that the toggle is what speeds things up — priority orders might simply tend to come from closer neighbourhoods.

When only observational data supports a finding, restate it as an association or a hypothesis to check later — not a causal claim. Instead of "using priority delivery causes faster delivery," write: "priority orders and faster delivery times tend to occur together in this data; whether the toggle itself speeds things up is worth checking further."

steps.title: Restate as an Association
steps.lede: Practise turning a causal claim into an honest association statement.

steps.title: Flag the Causal Claim
steps.lede: Given a set of findings about QuickShip deliveries, identify which ones make an unsupported causal claim and restate them as associations.

steps.title: What You've Learned
steps.lede: Three ideas to carry forward from this tile.

blocks.text: Correlation, always between −1 and +1, describes the strength and direction of a linear relationship. Read the sign for direction and the distance from 0 for strength. Rank multiple correlations by magnitude, not by the number itself. And when data is only observational, state findings as associations — never as causes.

blocks.title: Up Next: DataFrames and Series
blocks.text: In the next tile you'll meet the pandas DataFrame — the two-dimensional table structure that holds your data in Python, with rows and columns you can slice, filter, and transform.

remediation_steps.title: Positive vs. Negative: A Clear Contrast
remediation_steps.lede: Compare two QuickShip pairs side by side to see the difference between a positive and a negative association.

blocks.text: Distance and delivery time: correlation 0.82. As distance goes up, delivery time tends to go up too — that's a positive association. Package weight and delivery time: correlation −0.41. As weight goes up, delivery time tends to go down — that's a negative association. The sign alone tells you the direction.

remediation_steps.title: Confounding: One Variable Behind Two Others
remediation_steps.lede: See how a third variable can explain an association between two others.

blocks.text: Weight and delivery time have a correlation of −0.41. But distance is correlated with both: farther orders tend to be lighter parcels and also tend to take longer. So distance could be driving both sides of the weight–delivery-time association. A strong pairwise correlation never rules out a third variable behind both.

remediation_steps.title: Causal Claim vs. Association Statement
remediation_steps.lede: Compare a causal claim with its honest association restatement.

blocks.text: Causal claim: "Using the priority toggle causes faster delivery." Association restatement: "Priority orders and faster delivery times tend to occur together in this data; whether the toggle itself speeds things up is worth checking further." The restatement keeps the finding without claiming a cause the data can't prove.

tiles.title: Entities, Tables, and Primary Keys
tiles.summary: Recognise that a table models one kind of real-world thing, identify entities and their attributes in a business scenario, and select a valid primary key that is unique and never null.

steps.title: Every Table Represents One Real Thing
steps.lede: Before you design any table, you decide what real-world thing it is supposed to represent — that decision turns a business into a set of tables.

blocks.text: QuickShip has customers, orders, and products. Before writing a single column name, you have to decide: what real thing does each table represent? That decision is what turns a business into a set of tables in the first place.

An entity is an object in the real world with an independent existence that can be differentiated from other objects. It may have physical existence — a customer or a delivery driver — or conceptual existence, such as an order. Entities are defined as tables that hold specific information: the customers table holds data about the Customer entity; orders holds data about the Order entity.

blocks.title: QuickShip entities and their attributes
blocks.alt_text: Three entity boxes: Customer with attributes customer_id, name, city; Order with attributes order_id, customer_id, delivery_minutes; Product with attributes product_id, name. Each box groups the attributes of one real-world entity type.

blocks.text: An entity type defines a collection of similar entities — Customer is the entity type. The actual set of customer rows in the table right now is the entity set. Each entity is described by a set of attributes: Customer = (customer_id, name, city), just as Employee might be (Name, Address, Birthdate, Salary) in another business.

steps.title: Attributes of an Entity
steps.lede: Test your ability to list the attributes that describe a given entity.

steps.title: Identify Entities in the QuickShip Scenario
steps.lede: Given a description of the QuickShip business, match each real-world thing to an entity type and list its attributes.

steps.title: Picking the Column That Uniquely Identifies Every Row
steps.lede: Once customers is its own table, you need a way to point at exactly one customer row — name alone won't do.

blocks.text: Two customers could share a name. A phone number might be missing. A signup date might repeat. You need a column — or a combination of columns — whose values are unique and never null for every row in the table.

blocks.caption: Four candidate columns for the customers primary key. Only customer_id is unique and never null.

blocks.text: A primary key constraint indicates that a column, or group of columns, can be used as a unique identifier for the rows of a table; this requires the values to be both unique and not null. A table can have at most one primary key, and it can span more than one column — a composite key. For example, a table recording one row per (student_id, course_id) enrollment pair uses both columns together as the composite primary key.

steps.title: Entity Integrity
steps.lede: Test your understanding of what entity integrity requires.

steps.title: Select the Valid Primary Key
steps.lede: Given the QuickShip customers candidate-key table, select which column or columns can serve as the primary key.

steps.title: What You've Learned
steps.lede: Two ideas to carry forward from this tile.

blocks.text: Each table represents one kind of real-world thing — an entity — described by its attributes. Independent entities like Customer and Product can exist without depending on another table. Every table needs a primary key: a column or combination of columns that is unique and never null, guaranteeing entity integrity.

blocks.title: Up Next: Foreign Keys and One-to-Many Relationships
blocks.text: In the next tile you'll see how tables link to each other: a foreign key in the orders table points back to the exact customer row it belongs to, and you'll learn what happens when that pointer is left dangling.

remediation_steps.title: Attributes: What Describes One Entity
remediation_steps.lede: See the contrast between an entity type and the attributes that describe each instance.

blocks.text: Customer is the entity type. Each individual customer — Amara Okafor, Emeka Nwosu — is one entity instance. The attributes that describe every customer are customer_id, name, and city. Attributes belong to the entity type; values belong to each instance. Mixing up the type with its attributes is the most common early mistake.

remediation_steps.title: Why a Primary Key Must Never Be Null
remediation_steps.lede: See the contrast between a valid primary key and one that fails the null test.

blocks.text: customer_id: every row has a value, and no two rows share one — valid primary key. phone: customer 4 (Chidi Eze) has no phone number on record. A null in the primary key means you can't guarantee you're looking at exactly one customer. Entity integrity requires that neither the primary key nor any part of it contain null values.

tiles.title: Foreign Keys and One-to-Many Relationships
tiles.summary: Understand how a foreign key links a child table to a parent table, what referential integrity prevents, and how to identify the one side and the many side of a 1:M relationship.

steps.title: Linking Orders Back to the Right Customer
steps.lede: Every order belongs to some customer. The orders table needs a column that points back to the exact customer row — and a rule that keeps that pointer from dangling.

blocks.text: Every order in the orders table belongs to some customer. The orders table needs a way to point back to the exact customer row it belongs to, and to make sure that pointer is never left dangling.

blocks.title: Foreign key link: orders.customer_id → customers.customer_id
blocks.alt_text: Two table boxes: customers (customer_id PK, name, city) and orders (order_id PK, customer_id FK, delivery_minutes). An arrow runs from orders.customer_id to customers.customer_id. A third box shows an order row with customer_id = 99 whose arrow has no target in customers — an orphan record.

blocks.text: A foreign key constraint specifies that the values in a column (or group of columns) of one table must match values appearing in some row of another, referenced table. orders.customer_id is a foreign key referencing customers.customer_id — every customer_id value in orders must match an actual customer_id already in customers.

A null foreign key value satisfies referential integrity — an order with no customer_id at all doesn't violate the constraint. But a non-null value must match an existing primary key in the referenced table. A row whose foreign key value is not found in the referenced table is called an orphan record; referential integrity is what prevents these.

steps.title: Foreign Keys Build the Parent-Child Link
steps.lede: See how a foreign key value must already exist in the parent table, or the database refuses the insert.

steps.title: What Breaks Referential Integrity?
steps.lede: Test your understanding of what creates an orphan record.

steps.title: Find the Foreign Key and the Orphan
steps.lede: Given the QuickShip orders and customers tables, pick the foreign key column and identify which row value would break referential integrity.

steps.title: One Customer, Many Orders
steps.lede: A customer can place several orders, but each order belongs to at most one customer — that asymmetry has a name.

blocks.text: A customer can place several orders, but an order relates to at most one customer. That asymmetry between customers and orders is a specific, named kind of relationship.
In a one-to-many (1:M) relationship, one row on the 'one' side relates to many rows on the 'many' side — one department has many employees, and here, one customer has many orders.

blocks.title: One-to-many: customers (1) → orders (M)
blocks.alt_text: Two table boxes connected by a 1:M arrow. customers is the one side (customer_id PK). orders is the many side, with customer_id marked as the foreign key. The arrow points from customers to orders, showing one customer can have many orders.

blocks.text: A customer can place a minimum of zero and a maximum of many orders, while an order relates to a maximum of one customer — so orders is the many side. The foreign key customer_id is placed in the orders table and must match a valid customer_id in customers. A single customers row can't hold several order ids in one column, so the foreign key has to go on the many side.

steps.title: Telling One-to-Many from One-to-One
steps.lede: See how to decide which side is 'one' and which is 'many' by checking which side repeats the key.

steps.title: Where Does the Foreign Key Go?
steps.lede: Test your understanding of which table holds the foreign key in a 1:M relationship.

steps.title: Identify the One Side and the Many Side
steps.lede: Given the QuickShip customers and orders tables, identify which is the one side, which is the many side, and which table holds the foreign key.

steps.title: What You've Learned
steps.lede: Two ideas to carry forward from this tile.

blocks.text: A foreign key in the child table must match an existing primary key in the parent table — or be null. A non-null value with no match is an orphan record, and referential integrity prevents these. In a one-to-many relationship, the foreign key always lives on the many side: orders holds customer_id because one customer can have many orders, but an order belongs to only one customer.

blocks.title: Up Next: Normalization and Many-to-Many Relationships
blocks.text: In the next tile you'll see what happens when you store the same customer data on every order row — and how splitting tables into a normalised design, plus a junction table, solves that problem.

remediation_steps.title: Null vs. Non-Null Foreign Keys
remediation_steps.lede: See the contrast between a null foreign key (allowed) and a non-null one with no match (orphan).

blocks.text: Order 107 with customer_id = NULL: allowed — the constraint says a null value doesn't violate referential integrity. Order 107 with customer_id = 99: not allowed if no customer with id 99 exists in the customers table — that row becomes an orphan record. The rule is: non-null foreign key values must match an existing primary key in the referenced table.

remediation_steps.title: Why the Foreign Key Goes on the Many Side
remediation_steps.lede: See the contrast between storing the link on the one side versus the many side.

blocks.text: If you tried to store order ids in the customers table, one customer with three orders would need three order_id columns — or a repeating group. That breaks the table structure. Instead, each order row stores one customer_id. One customer row can match many order rows, but each order row points to exactly one customer. The foreign key always goes on the many side.

tiles.title: Normalization and Many-to-Many Relationships
tiles.summary: Learn why repeating data in a single table causes update anomalies, how splitting tables into separate entities removes that redundancy, and how a junction table resolves a many-to-many relationship into two ordinary one-to-many links.

steps.title: One big table — and its hidden cost
steps.lede: Imagine every order row repeating the customer's name and city. That design looks simple, but it carries a real cost.

blocks.text: Imagine, instead of separate customers and orders tables, one wide orders table that repeats each customer's name and city on every order row they place. A customer with five orders would have their name and city written out five separate times. Normalization is the process of determining how much redundancy exists in a table, with the goal of transforming the schema to remove that redundancy.

left.title: orders_flat (un-normalized)
left.alt_text: A single flat orders table with columns order_id, customer_name, customer_city, delivery_minutes. customer_name and customer_city are marked as repeating on every order row — the un-normalized design that causes update anomalies.

right.caption: customers table — name and city stored once; orders link back via customer_id

blocks.takeaway: Moving customer_name and customer_city into their own table stores each value exactly once. The orders table keeps only customer_id to link back — no more repeated values, no update anomaly.

steps.title: Update anomalies and the fix
steps.lede: Repeated data doesn't just waste space — it creates a consistency trap every time a value needs to change.

blocks.text: Redundant data is generally undesirable because it causes problems maintaining consistency after updates. If a customer's city changes, every one of the repeated rows must be updated. Missing even one leaves inconsistent data — an update anomaly, where the same customer appears to live in two different cities depending on which order row you read.

One way to remove the redundancy is to move the data that would otherwise repeat across many rows into a new, separate table, linked back to the original record by a key column — exactly the split into customers (name and city stored once each) and orders (which keeps only customer_id to identify the customer) that the QuickShip schema already uses.

steps.title: Splitting a table to remove redundancy
steps.lede: A single orders table stores customer_id, customer_name, customer_city, and delivery_minutes on every row. Which change removes the redundancy?

steps.title: Find the redundancy and redesign the table
steps.lede: The QuickShip orders table has customer details repeated on every row. Identify the redundant columns and redesign the schema into two tables that remove the update anomaly.

steps.title: When both sides can have many — the junction table
steps.lede: One order can include several products, and one product can appear in several orders. That shape of relationship needs a different solution.

blocks.text: One order can include several products, and one product — say, a rice bag — can show up in several different orders. Neither side is limited to 'one' the way customer/order was. A many-to-many (M:N) relationship cannot be implemented directly in the relational model; it is resolved into two one-to-many relationships using a composite entity, also called a junction or bridge table.

Between orders and products, that junction table — order_items — holds one row for every order/product pairing: order 101 paired with the rice bag, order 101 paired with cooking oil, order 103 paired with the rice bag again. Each pairing is its own row; the two sides connect through two one-to-many links.

blocks.title: Many-to-many resolved via order_items junction table
blocks.alt_text: ERD showing orders linked to order_items (1:N) and products linked to order_items (1:N). order_items has a composite primary key of order_id and product_id, both foreign keys. The many-to-many between orders and products is resolved through the junction table.

steps.title: What goes inside the junction table
steps.lede: The junction table must carry the right columns — and those columns together form its primary key.

blocks.text: The junction table must contain at least the primary keys of the two original tables, used as foreign keys, and may also contain additional attributes of its own. order_items holds order_id (a foreign key to orders) and product_id (a foreign key to products). The combination of those two foreign keys makes the primary key of the junction table — the pair (order_id, product_id) together is unique, since the same order won't list the same product twice.

steps.title: What you've learned
steps.lede: Two ideas that shape every well-designed relational schema.

blocks.text: Normalization removes redundancy by moving repeated data into its own table, linked back by a key — the customers/orders split is normalization already applied. When both sides of a relationship can have many, a junction table resolves it into two one-to-many links; order_items holds a foreign key to each side, and the pair of those keys forms the junction table's primary key.

remediation_steps.title: Splitting a table: a clear contrast
remediation_steps.lede: Compare a merged table with repeated values against the split design.

blocks.text: Un-normalized: one orders table with columns order_id, customer_name, customer_city, delivery_minutes. Customer Amara Okafor in Lagos appears on rows 101 and 103 — her city is stored twice. If she moves, both rows must be updated; missing one creates an update anomaly. Normalized: a customers table stores name and city once (customer_id 1 → Amara Okafor, Lagos). The orders table keeps only customer_id 1 on both rows — one update to customers fixes everything.

remediation_steps.title: Junction table keys: a clear contrast
remediation_steps.lede: Two designs — one missing a foreign key, one correct.

blocks.text: Incomplete: order_items has only order_id — it can't identify which product is in the order, so the link to products is broken. Correct: order_items has order_id (foreign key to orders) and product_id (foreign key to products). The pair (order_id, product_id) is the composite primary key — unique because the same order won't list the same product twice. Both foreign keys are required; either one alone is insufficient.

tiles.title: Reading ER Diagrams
tiles.summary: Learn to read an entity-relationship diagram: boxes for entity types, ovals for attributes with underlined primary keys, and marked relationship lines showing cardinality and connectivity.

steps.title: Boxes, ovals, and relationship lines
steps.lede: An entity-relationship diagram gives you a map of a schema — every entity, every attribute, and every relationship at a glance.

blocks.text: In an entity-relationship diagram (ERD), an entity type is represented by its name inside a box — Customer, Order, Product, and Order_Item would each get their own box. Each attribute is represented by an oval with its name inside, attached to its entity's box. The primary key attribute is shown by underlining it — customer_id, underlined, inside an oval attached to the Customer box.

An ERD shows relationships between entities as lines: one-to-one (1:1), one-to-many (1:M), and many-to-many (M:N). The Customer-to-Order line would be drawn as 1:M, matching that pair. Markings on a relationship line show cardinality and connectivity — the minimum and maximum number of related entities on each side. A three-pronged symbol means 'many'; a zero and one together mean 'zero or one'; a one-and-only-one symbol means that side is mandatory.

blocks.title: QuickShip ER diagram — customers, orders, products, order_items
blocks.alt_text: ERD with four entity boxes: Customer (customer_id underlined as PK, name, city), Order (order_id underlined as PK, customer_id FK, delivery_minutes), Order_Item (order_id FK+PK, product_id FK+PK), Product (product_id underlined as PK, name). Customer-to-Order line marked 1:M; Order-to-Order_Item marked 1:M; Product-to-Order_Item marked 1:M.

blocks.text: In an ERD, each entity type is a box, each attribute is an oval attached to its box, and the primary key attribute is underlined. Relationship lines show cardinality: a three-pronged symbol means 'many', a one-and-only-one symbol means mandatory, and a zero-and-one symbol means optional. Reading those markings tells you the minimum and maximum number of related entities on each side of every relationship.

remediation_steps.title: Cardinality markings: a clear contrast
remediation_steps.lede: Two relationship lines — one mandatory one-to-many, one optional.

blocks.text: Line A: Customer — Order, with a one-and-only-one symbol on the Customer side and a three-pronged symbol on the Order side. Reading: each order belongs to exactly one customer (mandatory), and one customer can have many orders. Line B: Customer — Order, with a zero-and-one symbol on the Customer side and a three-pronged symbol on the Order side. Reading: each order may belong to zero or one customer (optional). The symbol on each side tells you the minimum and maximum for that side — not the other.

tiles.title: Recommendations and Plain-Language Translation
tiles.summary: Learn to turn analytical findings into concrete recommendations using the 'because we found X, we recommend Y' pattern, and to rewrite technical results in plain language by glossing specialist terms and replacing formal words with simpler ones.

steps.title: From finding to action: the 'because X, recommend Y' pattern
steps.lede: A finding that sits in a report, unconnected to any suggested action, may not help the manager who needs to decide something.

blocks.text: Having found that Lagos delivery times rose, the next step is turning that finding into something the operations manager can act on. The value of analytical efforts is only truly realized when the insights discovered are acted upon — a finding that sits in a report, unconnected to any suggested action, may not do much for the manager who needs to decide something.

The pattern is: 'because we found X, we recommend Y.' For example: '...was successful and, because of the success, we recommend continuing to offer it going forward; please approve our budget for this program.' Following that same pattern for the delivery finding: 'because the average Lagos delivery time rose from 22 to 30 minutes this month, we recommend adding one more courier to the Lagos route.' The finding directly justifies the action.

steps.title: Replacing jargon and formal words
steps.lede: An analysis can accumulate technical terms that a non-technical manager won't follow. Two rules keep your writing clear.

blocks.text: Specialist terms can be used where needed — they are not always jargon — but explain them in plain English the first time they appear. If 'the average delivery time' needs to be called out as a mean for precision, saying 'the average (mean) delivery time' once keeps both the plain and the technical reader covered.

Formal or long words should be avoided when an easy or short one will do — for example 'buy' instead of 'purchase', 'help' instead of 'assist', 'about' instead of 'approximately'. Jargon and buzzwords should also be avoided because they are often vague and can be misinterpreted. 'Delivery times got worse this month' reads more plainly than 'delivery time performance exhibited negative variance this period.'

nodes.label: Technical: 'The mean delivery time exhibited a statistically significant increase of approximately 8 minutes, suggesting negative operational variance in the Lagos route.'

before.alt_text: A technically-worded sentence using 'mean', 'statistically significant', 'approximately', and 'negative operational variance'.

nodes.label: Plain: 'The average (mean) delivery time rose by about 8 minutes in Lagos this month — deliveries got slower.'

after.alt_text: The plain-language rewrite: 'mean' is glossed as 'average (mean)', 'approximately' becomes 'about', and 'negative operational variance' becomes 'got slower'.

blocks.change_summary: 'approximately' → 'about'; 'exhibited a statistically significant increase' → 'rose'; 'negative operational variance' → 'got slower'; 'mean' glossed as 'average (mean)' on first use.

blocks.text: Analytical value is only realized when findings lead to action. The 'because we found X, we recommend Y' pattern connects a specific finding directly to a concrete suggested action. Plain-language translation keeps the message accessible: gloss specialist terms on first use, and replace formal or long words with simpler equivalents — 'about' not 'approximately', 'help' not 'assist'.

remediation_steps.title: Data-grounded vs. ungrounded recommendation: a clear contrast
remediation_steps.lede: Two recommendations about Lagos delivery times — one grounded in data, one not.

blocks.text: Ungrounded: 'We should add more couriers to Lagos.' No finding is cited — the recommendation floats free of the data. Grounded: 'Because the average Lagos delivery time rose from 22 to 30 minutes this month, we recommend adding one more courier to the Lagos route.' The specific finding (22 → 30 minutes) directly justifies the specific action (one more courier). The 'because X, recommend Y' structure makes the link explicit.

remediation_steps.title: Plain language: a clear contrast
remediation_steps.lede: The same finding — one version technical, one plain.

blocks.text: Technical: 'The median (M = 26 min) was below the mean (M = 29.2 min), indicating positive skewness in the delivery-time distribution.' Plain: 'Most deliveries finished in about 26 minutes, but a few very slow orders pulled the average (mean) up to about 29 minutes — the data is skewed right.' Changes: 'M = 26 min' → 'about 26 minutes'; 'positive skewness' → 'skewed right'; 'mean' glossed as 'average (mean)' on first use; 'indicating' → dropped in favour of a plain causal phrase.

tiles.title: Tailoring Detail and Anticipating Questions
tiles.summary: Learn to adjust information density and presentation order for technical vs. executive audiences, and to anticipate stakeholder questions by answering them in the writing.

steps.title: Same Finding, Different Audiences
steps.lede: The Lagos delivery-time analysis might go to the operations manager or to the executive team. Both need the finding — but not the same amount of detail.

blocks.text: Designing with a specific person in mind helps avoid the 'mixed audience' trap. Knowing the audience's motivations lets you frame what they need to know or do in terms of those motivating factors. That knowledge should inform choices such as how much information density to include, and whether to add more context or explain something in greater detail.

steps.title: Technical vs. Big-Picture Audiences
steps.lede: The order in which you present findings and recommendations should shift depending on who is reading.

blocks.text: Technical or detail-oriented people may prefer to understand the specifics of an analysis first, so they are prepared to take in ideas about next steps. With executives or other big-picture-oriented people — who do not have a lot of patience for the specifics — you should think about starting with your request. An executive audience might only want the high-level arc: the operations manager may want the day-by-day breakdown, while the executive slide can lead with the recommendation and skip the breakdown.

steps.title: Answering Questions Before They Are Asked
steps.lede: Handing the operations manager a recommendation to add a Lagos courier is unlikely to be the end of the conversation.

blocks.text: An analyst should be prepared to respond to challenge from the approver, or scrutiny from project or programme boards, about their analysis. Being tailored to the audience means thinking about what questions they will ask, and answering these in the writing — so the Lagos report can note up front what else was ruled out (traffic patterns, order volume) before the manager has to ask.

Some technical or detail-oriented people prefer to understand the specifics of an analysis first, so they are prepared for ideas about next steps. Presenting findings before a request can, in that situation, avoid an audience derailing the presentation with a bunch of questions — showing the Lagos data before asking for budget approval can head off 'where's this number from' mid-request.

Technical audiences often want the analysis first; executives usually want the recommendation first. blocks.text: The operations manager wants to understand the analysis before hearing the recommendation — so the detail-first version opens with context (delivery times rose from 22 to 30 min), walks through the method, and ends with the ask. The executive wants the recommendation first and the high-level arc only — so the recommendation-first version leads with 'add one courier' and follows with the key finding. The structural difference is the signal: where the recommendation appears tells you which audience the version is written for.

tiles.title: Structuring Presentations and Writing Executive Summaries
tiles.summary: Learn to structure a short presentation as opening, body, and call to action, and to write an executive summary with a takeaway title and section headers.

steps.title: Opening, Body, Call to Action
steps.lede: With the Lagos finding, the recommendation, and a simplified chart ready, the last piece is putting them in an order that carries the operations manager from 'why am I reading this' to 'what do you want me to do.'

blocks.text: A summary should have an obvious beginning, middle, and end. In the beginning, level-set the audience; in the middle, present the analysis; in the end, conclude with the key takeaways. In a story's structure, the beginning establishes the context of the situation, and this gets carried onward to the twist, before the ending brings the story to its close. Mapped onto the Lagos presentation: the beginning is the situation (delivery times across the three cities this month), the twist is the Lagos slowdown, and the ending is the courier recommendation.

blocks.title: Three-Part Presentation Spine

nodes.label: Opening
nodes.detail: Context / situation — why are we reviewing Lagos delivery times?

nodes.label: Body
nodes.detail: Finding + evidence — Lagos avg delivery time rose from 22 to 30 min; distance is the strongest driver.

nodes.label: Call to Action
nodes.detail: What is being asked — approve adding one courier on the longest Lagos routes.

steps.title: Ending with a Call to Action
steps.lede: The presentation closes by asking the audience for something — once they have the context to understand the request.

blocks.text: A presentation can end with a call to action, stating what is being asked of the audience, once the audience has the context needed to understand the request — so the Lagos presentation can open with why the review happened, move through the finding and chart, and close by asking management to approve one added courier.

steps.title: The Executive Summary: One Page That Must Stand Alone
steps.lede: The full Lagos delivery-time presentation may never get read past its first page.

blocks.text: An executive summary is a one- or two-page overview of a much longer presentation, provided so the reader gets the main messages without reading the entire communication; it may be the only thing the audience ever looks at. The summary's title should state the main takeaway and set the tone for the rest of the page, and the summary should follow a narrative arc with an obvious beginning, middle, and end — a title like 'Lagos delivery times are slowing — recommend adding one courier' already tells a skimming reader the point before they read a word of the body.

Content should be grouped into easily-discernible sections with text headers, so someone scanning for only a few seconds still understands the main points. Bullets should generally be avoided in favour of well-constructed sentences and mini-paragraphs, except when listing elements. A short 'Finding' section and a short 'Recommendation' section, each a sentence or two, serve a scanning reader better than a single unbroken paragraph.

before.title: Before: unstructured paragraph

nodes.label: Single unbroken paragraph: 'Lagos delivery times rose from 22 to 30 minutes in Month 2. Distance is the strongest driver (r=0.82). We recommend adding one courier on the longest routes. Traffic patterns and order volume were ruled out as primary causes. The analysis covered 20 orders across Lagos, Abuja, and Kano.'

before.alt_text: Before: one unbroken paragraph with no title, no section headers, mixing finding, recommendation, and method.

Recommendation: Add one courier on the longest Lagos routes to bring average delivery time back below 25 minutes.

steps.title: Presentation Structure and Executive Summaries — Key Takeaways

blocks.text: Structure every presentation as opening (context), body (finding + evidence), and call to action (what you are asking). An executive summary is a one- or two-page overview that may be the only thing the audience reads; its title should state the main takeaway, and content should be grouped under section headers in prose, not bullets.

remediation_steps.title: Opening, Body, Call to Action — The Three Slots
remediation_steps.lede: Every presentation has three jobs to do, in order.

blocks.text: The opening level-sets the audience: why are we looking at Lagos delivery times? The body presents the finding and the evidence: delivery times rose from 22 to 30 minutes in Month 2, and distance is the strongest driver. The call to action closes the presentation by stating what is being asked — approve adding one courier — only after the audience has the context needed to understand the request. Placing the call to action before the context leaves the audience without the 'why', making the request harder to evaluate.
